_note: Sites: somewhere to go that is not a port. No market, no fuel, no docking; you arrive on site and work. 'location' is as for places. 'visibility': known (on the map from the start), rumour (heard through tips), or hidden (only by story or contract). Each activity: needs (module abilities: survey, lander, mining), days of work, risk (chance it goes wrong: less yield, and for landings a fuel cost), yields (goods tonnes [min, max], into the hold as room allows), credits (paid on completion, e.g. survey data sold by radio), rep ({operator: amount}), and text for the result. 'once': worked out after one go.

ishikawa_maru.name: Derelict: Ishikawa Maru
ishikawa_maru.description: A Cooperative ice tanker that lost its drive controller in '58 and was left in a high lunar orbit, crew safe, cargo not. Salvage rights lapsed last year. Whoever gets there first.

salvage.name: Strip the wreck
salvage.text: Two days in suits with cutters and a cargo net. Her controller was fried, but the pumps are good.

hermes_probe.name: Dead probe: Hermes-7
hermes_probe.description: A deep-space relay that went silent in 2049 and has drifted ever since on a long, lazy orbit four times the Moon's distance out. The inquiry blamed a cosmic ray. Nobody ever went and got the recorder.

salvage.name: Recover the memory core
salvage.text: She isn't wrecked. No impact, no debris: the wings are folded, the battery cleanly isolated, the instruments capped, a textbook safe-mode shutdown done perfectly, like someone put her to bed. Only the high-gain antenna is wrong: it should point home, and it points at an empty patch of sky. You bring the memory core in by hand. It's scorched along one edge, and partly corrupted.

eros_survey.name: Eros
eros_survey.description: A 34 km near-Earth asteroid, stony and well mapped from orbit but never properly surveyed for what is under the regolith. The Belt Assembly buys good survey data.

survey.name: Survey from orbit
survey.text: Six days of radar passes and spectrometry. The data goes out by radio as you finish.

prospect.name: Land and core
prospect.text: The lander goes down on the saddle, drills three cores and comes back up dusty.

psyche_deep_claim.name: Psyche, the eastern claim
psyche_deep_claim.description: An unclaimed patch on Psyche's far side where the old Psyche mission's magnetometer saw something odd. The claimants say it is nothing. They have not been to look.

mine.name: Set up the rig and mine
mine.text: Ten days of drilling. The magnetometer was right: a pocket of platinum-group metal ten metres down.

phobos_survey.name: Phobos
phobos_survey.description: Mars' inner moon, 22 km of rubble spiralling slowly in. The Accord wants to know whether it is worth mining before it falls.

survey.name: Survey from orbit
survey.text: Four days of passes over the grooves. The data goes to the Accord as you finish.

prospect.name: Land at Stickney
prospect.text: Down into Stickney crater, where the shadowed walls hold ice.

hektor_survey.name: Hektor
hektor_survey.description: The largest of Jupiter's Trojans: two lobes, 225 km end to end, and almost unknown. Whoever surveys it first sets the claims map for the whole neighbourhood.

survey.name: Survey both lobes
survey.text: Ten days mapping the neck between the lobes. The Commons buys the map at once; the Belt Assembly pays to see it.

the_lacuna.name: The Lacuna
the_lacuna.description: A thousand AU out, past Sedna's long orbit: a sphere a few kilometres across that reflects nothing at all. Stars behind it vanish; stars beside it bend. It was here before the array looked, and probably before anyone looked at anything.

greet.name: Go and say hello
greet.text: You close to fifty kilometres and send the oldest greeting there is: a count, one to ten. For two days, nothing. Then your own count comes back, in your own voice, from all around the sky at once.

halley_watch.name: Halley's Comet
halley_watch.description: The comet everyone has heard of, back for the first time since 1986. It falls past the Sun on 28 July 2061 going the wrong way round, so matching it costs more than any trip in the system. The few who get here will tell their grandchildren. Keep outside the coma, and take your time.

watch.name: Sample the coma from standoff
watch.text: Five days riding alongside at four hundred kilometres, sniffing the gas and catching dust on aerogel. Giotto saw this nucleus for a few seconds at 68 km/s. You get to watch it breathe. The data goes home by radio, and half the system tunes in.

dive.name: Dive through the inner coma
dive.text: Two days down among the jets, hull pinging like hail on a tin roof, star trackers lost in the glitter. You come out with a hold full of the oldest ice there is and a ship that needs a wash.

land.name: Land on the nucleus
land.text: Halley's nucleus is blacker than coal and as light as a snowdrift. You anchor with harpoons, as Philae meant to, and bring up ice that has been frozen since before there were planets.

comet_67p_claim.name: 67P: Rosetta's comet
comet_67p_claim.description: The rubber-duck comet Rosetta orbited for two years. Four kilometres of dusty ice on a six-and-a-half-year loop out to Jupiter's orbit. Asleep for most of the decade, which makes it the best homestead ice in the inner system, as long as you are gone, or dug in, when it wakes.

survey.name: Survey both lobes
survey.text: Five days of radar sounding through the neck. The cliffs Rosetta photographed have slumped and moved; the claims office buys the new map.

prospect.name: Land at Agilkia and core
prospect.text: Down where Philae first bounced. You have better harpoons. Three cores of dirty ice, all of it going spare.

mine.name: Set up the rig and mine ice
mine.text: Twelve days at the rig in the Hapi valley, where the ice is closest. Water is the most useful thing there is out here, and this comet is mostly water.

sample.name: Sample the waking coma
sample.text: Four days at standoff as the jets switch on with the dawn. Rosetta's team asked questions about this comet's water that are still open. Your data answers two of them.

bennu_survey.name: Bennu
bennu_survey.description: The rubble-pile asteroid OSIRIS-REx touched in 2020 and found it was barely a solid at all: the sampler sank in like a ball pit. Carbon-rich, a little water in its clays, and an easy trip from Earth.

survey.name: Map it boulder by boulder
survey.text: Three days of close passes. Bennu has shed a little more gravel since 2020; the Compact wants to know where it went.

prospect.name: Touch and go
prospect.text: A touch and a puff of gas, as OSIRIS-REx did, then a quick back-off before the surface swallows the pad. A sack of dark, hydrated gravel.

ryugu_survey.name: Ryugu
ryugu_survey.description: The spinning-top asteroid Hayabusa2 shot a crater into in 2019. Dark, carbon-rich and full of hydrated clays. A good first place to learn to mine on a small world, a short hop from Earth.

survey.name: Survey from orbit
survey.text: Three days of passes. The crater Hayabusa2 made is still there, sharp-edged in the low gravity.

mine.name: Set up the rig and mine
mine.text: Eight days drilling clays near the equator ridge. Bake them and they give up their water.

dart_crater.name: Didymos and the DART crater
dart_crater.description: In 2022 the DART spacecraft hit Didymos' little moon Dimorphos on purpose and changed its orbit: the first time people moved a world to show they could protect their own. Dimorphos still circles Didymos every 11 hours 23 minutes, half an hour faster than before. Visitors come to see where.

survey.name: Survey the impact site
survey.text: Two days mapping the scar on Dimorphos and the debris it threw into orbit. The planetary defence office buys the data every decade, to see how a nudged world settles.

visit.name: Pay your respects
visit.text: Half a day holding station over the crater. Someone left a small plaque in orbit: a list of the DART team, and under it, 'We could, so we did.'

slow_tide_berg.name: Berg in transit: the Slow Tide
slow_tide_berg.description: A berg of water ice the size of a cathedral, pushed in from the Themis family by the pusher Slow Tide and bound for the Kernel. Its crew of five live in a cabin bolted to the pusher's frame, a year and a half out from the Belt, and they melt and throw a little of their own berg every hour to keep it coming. They can't stop for shopping. Anyone who flies out with fresh food, medicine and spare parts is the most welcome person in the system, and they pay, and they top up your hold from the berg.

resupply.name: Bring the crew their supplies
resupply.text: Half a day matched with the berg, passing crates across on a line. They cook you the first fresh meal they've had in four months, and send you off with a few tonnes of ice chipped from the berg.
